chunk_findings.detail: `git diff --name-only` output parsed with `.splitlines()` is not path-safe under Git’s default `core.quotepath` setting. In a freshly initialized repo, a changed file such as `café.py` is printed as the quoted string `"caf\303\251.py"`; feeding that to `globs.match(f, g)` with a glob like `**/*.py` returns `False`. For `started_on=A`, `newer=B`, and `paths=["**/*.py"]`, where `B` changed `café.py`, `superseded_by` would incorrectly return `False`, so a stale gate result can be recorded. Use `-z` and split on NULs, or `-c core.quotepath=false`, instead of parsing quoted `--name-only` output.

chunk_findings.detail: The fix scopes every gate’s superseded check by the current item’s `globs` (`paths=(it.globs if it else None)`). That under-scopes whole-tree gates such as `ci`, which the bug report itself describes as the full pre-push suite. Concretely: with item globs `["mine.py"]`, `ci` passes on commit A; descendant commit B changes `other.py` to introduce a suite-breaking error. `superseded_by(A, B, cwd, paths=["mine.py"])` now returns `False` — indeed the new test asserts exactly that — so A’s pass is treated as still valid even though the whole tree has moved. Then `unit_tests` can be allowed on a tree where the whole suite has not actually passed. The fix should scope by the gate’s own coverage or exclude `.ddflow/events`, not by the item’s files.

chunk_findings.detail: When `r.kept_stash` is truthy, the same `r.detail` text is appended to `text` after `text = _text(r, data)`, even though `data` already contains `"detail": r.detail` and `_text` is the component that renders refusal/conflict details. In a keep_local sync where restoring the stash conflicts, `r.status` is `"conflict"` and `r.kept_stash` can be true; the resulting refusal message will contain the conflict detail twice. The append should be limited to successful kept-stash outcomes whose `_text` does not already include `r.detail`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/lifecycle/sync.py:62-63

chunk_findings.detail: `_stash_back` drops the stash using the reflog selector captured earlier from `_stash_find` (`stash@{n}`). That selector is not stable when another worktree/session pushes a stash in between, because `git stash push` inserts the new entry at `stash@{0}` and renumbers older entries. Interleaving: session A stashes/tags its work, merges, then `_stash_find` returns `stash@{0}` for A; before A runs `git stash drop stash@{0}`, session B (same repo, different worktree) runs `git stash push`; A’s saved selector now refers to B’s stash, so A drops B’s uncommitted work and leaves A’s stale stash in place. This is the shared-stash race the new `_stash_away` comment acknowledges, but the drop is not protected against it.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/branchsync.py:_stash_back

chunk_findings.detail: The new stale_rules refusal message concatenates two adjacent string literals without a separating space: the line ending in `"puts"` followed by the line starting with `f"back; ...“` renders as `"...which it sets aside and putsback; or `git merge ...`"`. This is the exact user-facing text shown to an agent escaping a dirty-tree stale_rules refusal, and the malformed word is wrong output for that input.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/enforce.py:2248

chunk_findings.detail: `_stash_back` applies the stash by SHA, then separately runs `_stash_find(tag)` and later `git stash drop ref` using the returned `stash@{n}`. The stash stack is shared across worktrees, and another session can push a new stash between the `_stash_find` subprocess and the `git stash drop` subprocess. Concrete interleaving: session A creates its entry at `stash@{0}` and applies it; `_stash_find` returns `stash@{0}`; session B then pushes a new stash, so B is now `stash@{0}` and A becomes `stash@{1}`; A's subsequent `git stash drop stash@{0}` deletes B's stashed work while A's entry remains. This is data loss of another worktree's uncommitted work, and the code's own comment acknowledges that other sessions may push meanwhile.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/branchsync.py:_stash_back

chunk_findings.detail: `if r.kept_stash:` appends the “kept in stash” note regardless of `r.status`. In the keep_local conflict path, `r.status == "conflict"` and `r.kept_stash` can be true (the stash apply conflicted with the new base). The output then tells the user that `git stash apply <r.kept_stash>` “puts it back,” but the stash has already been applied and the worktree is dirty with conflict markers; re-running that command fails with Git’s “Cannot apply to a dirty working tree” instead of recovering the work. The note should be limited to successful kept-stash outcomes or reworded for the conflict state.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/lifecycle/sync.py:65

chunk_findings.detail: The stale-selector race from the previous HIGH finding still exists in the recovery path. After `_drop` detects it dropped the wrong stash, it restores that stranger's entry, re-finds ours by sha, and then runs `W.git(tree, "stash", "drop", again)` with a freshly-captured `stash@{n}` selector. That second drop is not checked against `sha`. If another worktree pushes a stash between `_stash_find(tree, sha)` and the second drop, `again` shifts and the second drop deletes the new or just-restored stranger's stash with no recovery, causing data loss. The added test covers a single concurrent push, but not a push during this recovery re-find/drop window, so the fix does not fully answer the prior report.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/branchsync.py:_drop

chunk_findings.detail: When `ddflow sync --keep-local` succeeds at the base merge but `_stash_back` then fails to restore the stashed uncommitted work, `_restore` leaves `out.status` as `"merged"` (set immediately before the call). Concrete input: an uncommitted edit to `foo.txt`, while `rep.base` also edits the same lines. `_stash_away` stashes the edit, `git merge` then fast-forwards cleanly, and `_stash_back` applies the stash with a conflict. The function appends `detail` and sets `kept_stash`, but still returns `status: "merged"`, telling callers the sync completed while the worktree has conflict markers and the user’s uncommitted work is still only in the stash. The result status should indicate the restore conflict/failure, not `"merged"`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/branchsync.py:_restore

chunk_findings.detail: The newly added regression test for the confirmed HIGH finding does not actually exercise the code path that held the bug: it never calls `BS._stash_back`. It calls `BS._drop(wt, ref, mine)` directly. As written, a `_stash_back` implementation that again drops the earlier-returned reflog selector after another stash push would leave this test green, because `_stash_back` is not executed. The probe should drive `_stash_back` (or `sync`) through the interleaving, or otherwise assert that `_stash_back` does not drop the other session’s `tag-theirs`; testing only `_drop` does not guard the reported defect.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_sync_keep_local.py:70 test_a_stash_pushed_meanwhile_by_another_worktree_is_not_dropped

chunk_findings.detail: Previous finding [1] still holds: the fix only verifies the first `git stash drop` in `_drop`, but the recovery path then does `_stash_find(tree, sha)` followed by an **unchecked** `git stash drop again`. Concrete interleaving: A’s `_stash_find(tag_A)` returns `stash@{0}`; B pushes, so B is `stash@{0}` and A is `stash@{1}`; `_drop` drops B, detects B != A, stores B back; `_stash_find(sha_A)` now finds A at `stash@{1}`; C pushes, making C `stash@{0}`, B `stash@{1}`, and A `stash@{2}`; the final `git stash drop stash@{1}` then drops B again, with no verification or restoration, so B’s stashed work is silently lost while `_stash_back` returns success. The guard would need to be applied to this second drop as well, or the entry should be dropped by immutable SHA.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/branchsync.py:_drop (final `W.git(tree, "stash", "drop", again)`)

chunk_findings.detail: The diff has not answered the earlier race: the new `--keep-local` path still calls `_stash_back` from `_restore`, and no locking or direct drop-by-stash-SHA mechanism is added. In the concrete interleaving already reported, session A creates its stash at `stash@{0}`, applies it by SHA, `_stash_find(tag)` resolves it to `stash@{0}`, then session B pushes a new stash so A’s entry becomes `stash@{1}`; A next drops `stash@{0}` and silently deletes B’s stash while A’s own applied stash remains. That remains possible because the stash stack is shared across worktrees.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/branchsync.py:_stash_back

chunk_findings.detail: The test added as the regression for the `_stash_back` race never calls `_stash_back`; it directly calls `_stash_away`, `_stash_find`, and the newly added `BS._drop`. The bug from the earlier finding is specifically the interleaving inside `_stash_back`: after `_stash_find` resolves the selector, another session pushes a stash before `_stash_back` runs `git stash drop ref`. Because this test’s interleaving happens around a direct `_drop` call, a still-buggy `_stash_back` that continued to run `git stash drop ref` directly would not be exercised, so the test can pass while the race remains. It therefore does not act as the intended red test for B-stale-rules-escape-needs-file-copy.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_sync_keep_local.py:test_a_stash_pushed_meanwhile_by_another_worktree_is_not_dropped
